rejected.title: Tsunamis
card: A tsunami is a series of huge waves that floods coasts. It is not a single wave.
Most tsunamis are set off by an undersea earthquake. The sea floor suddenly lifts or drops and moves the water above it.
The waves can cross a whole ocean and flood coasts thousands of kilometres from where the tsunami started.
In deep water the waves are low and hard to notice. Near the coast they slow down and rise, and water can surge far inland.
rejected.remember: A tsunami is a set of waves usually set off by a sudden jolt to the sea floor, and it can hit far-away coasts.

a.q: What usually sets off a tsunami?
opts: An undersea earthquake that moves the sea floor
Strong winds blowing across the open ocean
The pull of the Moon on the sea at high tide
A cyclone moving towards the coast
a.why: A sudden movement of the sea floor pushes the water above it and starts the waves. Strong winds make ordinary waves, not tsunamis, even when the sea looks rough.
a.clue: Think about what suddenly moves the water from below.

b.q: An undersea earthquake strikes near Chile. Hours later, waves flood a harbour in Japan, and the sea was calm there when the earthquake happened. What best explains this?
opts: The tsunami waves travelled across the ocean
The earthquake shook the harbour directly
Local winds in Japan whipped up large waves
The tide in Japan happened to be very high
b.why: A tsunami is a series of waves that can cross an ocean and flood coasts far from where it started. The harbour was calm at first because the waves had not yet arrived. By the time the earthquake's shaking reaches Japan, it is far too weak to cause flooding.
b.clue: Notice how many hours passed before the water arrived.

problems.detail: The card says 'most' tsunamis come from undersea earthquakes, but the remember line defines every tsunami as coming 'from a sudden jolt to the sea floor'. It drops the qualifier, though landslides and volcanic eruptions can also cause tsunamis. Add 'usually'.
The clue says 'something must have travelled', which echoes the word 'travelled' in the right option and gives the answer away.

The why says 'Shaking from the earthquake does not reach that far.' Seismic waves from a large Chilean earthquake do reach Japan and can be recorded there, just not as damaging shaking, and they arrive within minutes, not hours. Reword to say the shaking is too weak that far away to cause flooding.
